query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a low-density, refractory element such as Ti or Al into the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce its density without sacrificing its strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Addition of a low-density, refractory element such as Ti or Al
generation.conditions: Room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1000 °C
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a uniform, fine lamellar microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix
generation.mechanism: The added low-density element will reduce the overall density of the alloy while maintaining its high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility due to the formation of a stable, coherent BCC + B2 microstructure
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room-temperature fracture toughness and reduced density without sacrificing high-temperature yield strength
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g cm−3 and yield strength of 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at 1000 °C
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C; loading conditions: uniaxial tension and compression
generation.uncertainty: The exact effect of the added low-density element on the alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties is uncertain and requires experimental verification

falsification_experiment.design: Cast and characterize the microstructure and mechanical properties of the modified HfMoTaTiZr alloy with added low-density element
measurements: Yield strength at room temperature and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy exhibits a significant decrease in yield strength or fracture toughness at room temperature, or a significant increase in density, then the hypothesis is falsified

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties
